query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles, the onset and gradual progression of the premelting and melting process are governed by local reductions in melting temperature at the nanoparticle surfaces due to nanoscale surface energy effects coupled with slight compositional fluctuations. These factors create ‘premelting sites’ at the particle surfaces that initiate melting and then propagate inward, with the effect being more pronounced in smaller particles.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, single‐phase homogeneous FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles that may exhibit minor compositional fluctuations but overall a solid solution structure.
generation.intervention: Controlled heating under an inert atmosphere (e.g., argon) with a well‐defined, moderate heating rate, while comparing nanoparticles of different average sizes.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed in an inert environment to avoid oxidation; using samples with distinct but well‐characterized size distributions (e.g., ultrasmall ~5 nm versus larger ~50 nm particles) and a controlled heating rate (e.g., 5 K/min) that traverses the premelting and melting regime.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoscale variation in surface energy and local compositional heterogeneity (even if slight) at the particle surfaces that lower the effective melting point locally.
generation.mechanism: Due to the high surface-to-volume ratio, regions at the nanoparticle surfaces possess higher surface energy and are more sensitive to local compositional variations. These regions have a reduced local melting point relative to the particle interior. When heated, these surface sites undergo premelting, creating liquid domains that gradually coalesce and propagate inward, resulting in a full phase transition. Smaller nanoparticles, having a larger fraction of atoms at or near the surface, will show an earlier and more gradual melting onset.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical heating conditions, smaller nanoparticles will begin to show signatures of surface premelting (e.g., via DTA/DSC endothermic peaks or in situ TEM contrast changes) at lower temperatures compared to larger ones. The progression from partial (surface) melting to full melting will occur over a broader temperature range in smaller particles relative to the baseline of the homogeneous solid-phase state.
generation.baseline: A solid, homogeneous high-entropy alloy nanoparticle with a uniform crystal lattice and no premelted regions at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies when the nanoparticles are heated in an inert atmosphere using controlled heating ramps so that extrinsic effects (e.g., oxidation or uncontrolled agglomeration) are minimized. The effect is expected to be most pronounced in well-dispersed nanoparticles with minimal extraneous impurities.
generation.uncertainty: The exact numerical onset temperatures are uncertain due to the lack of direct measurements for FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles; the hypothesis extrapolates size- and surface-energy-related effects observed in other HEA nanoparticle studies (e.g., PMC7956699 and PMC8797181) to this system. What is new in this proposal is combining nanoparticle size as a controlled variable with the idea that even minimal compositional modulation at the surface drives premelting, which has not been directly tested in this specific alloy system.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two distinct ensembles of FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles with well-characterized, significantly different average sizes (e.g., ~5 nm and ~50 nm). Subject both ensembles to identical heating profiles using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and perform in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) during heating under an inert atmosphere. Compare the onset of premelting (e.g., appearance of endothermic events, surface blurring or contrast changes in TEM) for the different sizes.
measurements: DSC/DTA curves to determine the onset temperature and rate of heat absorption changes associated with premelting and melting.
In situ TEM imaging to directly observe surface premelting and the progression of the liquid phase within nanoparticles.
Particle size distributions pre- and post-heating to verify that size differences correlate with differences in thermal behavior.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the two nanoparticle ensembles do not show a statistically significant difference in the onset or progression of premelting/melting (i.e., if both sizes transition at the same temperatures and with similar progression profiles), this would falsify the hypothesis that nanoscale surface energy effects and concomitant local compositional variations are governing the thermal phase transitions.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, thermal analysis of the CoCrFeMo0.85Ni HEA powder was carried out via differential thermal analysis (DTA) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to assess the thermodynamic properties of HEA, including the solidus, liquidus and phase transition temperatures. With detailed characterization of microstructures in the DTA sample, the critical temperatures determined in thermal analysis can be correlated with microstructural features to examine phase formation and formation of precursor states from compositional modulations in HEA. This will provide fundamental understanding on intermetallic strengthening mechanism and phase stability for processing of HEAs.

We attribute the size effect on the disorder-to-order transition to the difference in surface energy. MPEIs have a lower surface energy than HEAs, as MPEIs forms stronger atom-atom interactions (). Because of the large relative surface area of small nanoparticles, we hypothesize that the difference in the surface energy between MPEI and HEA small nanoparticles (~5 nm) play a key role in driving the disorder-to-order transition. It is also possible that the larger particles (e.g., 10 to 20 nm) need to overcome a higher energy barrier to complete the disorder-to-order transition (). For the particles substantially larger than 5 nm (e.g., 150 nm), such a large energy barrier could hinder the formation of fully ordered MPEIs. The disorder-to-order transition is thermodynamically favored to form phase-stable MPEI nanoparticles. cited_evidence.text: The presence of different size fractions in the colloids that were produced can be assigned to distinct particle formation mechanisms in the picosecond-pulsed laser synthesis of colloids. Whereas ultrasmall NPs originate from nucleation and condensation in a low-density mixing region of the ablated metal species and the liquid environment in a supercritical state, larger NPs emerge from a highly dynamic molten layer on the surface of the ablation target due to Rayleigh–Taylor instability. However, the main product of the picosecond-pulsed laser ablation consisted of ultrasmall NPs, predicted to be formed in the low-density region. The small hydrodynamic diameters of laser-generated NPs result from fast kinetics. Cooling rates of the condensates in the order of 1012 K s−1 can be expected, and passivation of the surface of the NPs that occurs by the interaction with solvent species suppresses further growth.
